target_customer: Software and security teams at tech companies, enterprises and defense or critical infrastructure organizations
problem: AI coding agents ship code faster than security teams can audit it, and attackers can use AI to find bugs too. Companies need continuous vulnerability finding and fixing that keeps pace.
business_model: Open-source harness deployed and run for enterprises, plus a paid continuous testing product (0cloud) that opens fix pull requests, with a credit offer of 50 free PRs
product_category: AI offensive security and automated vulnerability remediation

founders.name: Doruk Tan Ozturk
prior_employers: Swiss retail conglomerate (cyber defense engineer, unnamed on YC page)
founders.background_notes: YC page also lists Chief Engineer for Cyber and Autonomous Systems on the Swiss Mars Rover team. Education not listed.

founders.name: Fabian Zbinden
prior_employers: Crypto Finance (early hire, later sold to Deutsche Borse)
founders.background_notes: Education not listed on the YC page.

competitors.what: Autonomous AI pentesting for web apps and APIs
competitors.traction_then: topped the HackerOne leaderboard in 2025 per vendor comparisons
competitors.funding_then: reported 120M in March 2026 by one comparison

competitors.name: MindFort
competitors.what: AI pentesting that opens fix pull requests
competitors.traction_then: pricing from 1,000 per month per its own buyers guide
competitors.funding_then: 3M plus round led by Soma Capital reported April 2026 by aggregator

technical_complexity.rationale: Agents that find, verify and patch vulnerabilities down to the Linux kernel need deep security research and reliable exploit verification. The company claims 30 plus kernel zero-days, which is a hard result for a two-person team.

defensibility.rationale: Open sourcing the harness limits code secrecy, but a track record of real CVEs and enterprise and defense relationships are hard to copy quickly.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Not yet known. Funded AI pentesting rivals were already shipping similar products at the time of the batch.

market_need_then: AI generated code is increasing the volume of unaudited software, and reports in 2026 describe models exposing vulnerabilities faster than teams patch them.

branding.domain_note: Uses 0.security (a TLD name) for the site; a second domain 0sec.ai appears as a contact address; the GitHub org is 0sec-labs.

identity.logo: Not described by any source found
identity.visual_style: Terminal and hacker aesthetic implied; Made in Switzerland, refined in San Francisco tagline
identity.voice_and_tone: Confident and technical, headline claim of fixes not findings

branding.brand_signature: The zero prefix name and the claim of ships fixes, not findings
branding.community_and_virality: Open-source release discussed in an X thread on 2026-11-08 and covered by small outlets; an earlier open-source engine was called pwnkit.

brand_strength.rationale: Early stage. Press mentions are small and the name is easily confused with 0sec and Zero Security style names, though it is short and memorable to security engineers.

outcome_analysis: The company is in its first months after the Fall 2026 batch. It claims real kernel vulnerabilities and an open-source launch, and lists enterprise and defense relationships, but no round, revenue or exit is verified. Direct competitors have raised far larger rounds, so the outcome is open.
notes: No funding source found; Dealroom page exists but figures not seen. Customer logos and the 30 plus kernel zero-day and 500 plus CVE claims come from the company and one small outlet and are unverified. The founders' education is not listed. Competitors are dated 2026 vendor comparisons, which are partly marketing.
